title: Singers take over and the end of orchestral dance music
summary: He admires Sinatra's arrangers, says singers took over after dance bands faded, and ends his story.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: For instance, like the bands behind Sinatra -- beautiful. He's a fine talent --
Well, Axel was very good too. No, the guy that does it now.
: Oh, I know who you mean, but I just can't think of it.
: Well, anyway, his orchestrations are beautiful.
And you take a guy like Sinatra, he don't have anything else. Even Andy Williams -- they're singers. But they can afford to go along with big bands,
beautiful instrumental sound, and they don't have more than one, two arrangers. But not everybody can work for those guys.
I would like to have been able to do that, because singers -- we got away from orchestral dance music.

And the singers took over. Everything was a vocal. You had to do a vocal. And by the time you're working here with an orchestral dance band, somebody else a lot of times has got ahead of you, let's say, and he's working with like a Sinatra singer, one of the singers that's taken over, and he's doing very well -- Perry Como, all those guys. They always had nice, big bands, beautiful big orchestral sounds to work with. And you never got away from it.

They didn't come in with, you know, behind the Beatles' stuff. But that's -- I don't take anything away from that. The business as I see it was due for a rhythmic change, and although the early Latins brought the eight-to-the-bar and four-to-the-bar in, it wasn't four-to-the-bar; it was eight-to-the-bar, you know, their type of doing it, but the melding of the thing, it took a while to do.
So that's -- that's my story, Mr. Agony.
